questions.prompt: Why does a password reset fail to remove illicit OAuth consent grant access?
options: Password resets take 24 hours to propagate to applications
The application holds tokens the user authorized -- no credential was ever stolen, so rotating the credential is irrelevant
OAuth grants are stored on the attacker's server
The reset must be performed twice
questions.explanation: The user never typed a password into anything attacker-controlled. Access derives from an authorization they granted, which persists independently of the credential.

questions.prompt: Which OAuth scope specifically converts access into durable persistence?
options: offline_access, which grants a refresh token allowing indefinite renewal without the user present
questions.explanation: Without offline_access, access tokens expire quickly. With it, the application can obtain new tokens indefinitely, which is what makes the grant persistence rather than a temporary session.

questions.prompt: What makes the illicit consent grant attack effective against security-aware users?
options: It uses a convincing fake login page
The consent page is the real Microsoft page, at a genuine Microsoft domain with a valid certificate -- there is nothing visually wrong to notice
It exploits a vulnerability in OAuth 2.0
It requires no user interaction at all
questions.explanation: Because the mechanism is used honestly rather than spoofed, the usual phishing indicators -- wrong domain, bad certificate, odd URL -- are all absent.

questions.prompt: What three steps are required to fully remediate an illicit consent grant?
options: Reset the password, enable MFA, and notify the user
Remove the permission grant, disable or delete the service principal, and revoke the user's refresh tokens
Delete the mailbox rules and reset the password
Block the sender and purge the phishing message
questions.explanation: Removing the grant alone can leave already-issued tokens valid until expiry, so all three steps are needed to actually terminate access.
